content: Poison control centers are accessible toll-free in most countries, operating 24/7 throughout the year. Following World War II, the rapid introduction of new drugs and chemicals into the market led to a significant rise in both accidental and intentional poisonings, particularly among children. During this period, poisonings accounted for nearly half of all childhood accidents, with many resulting in fatalities. In response, the medical community began developing systems to address these issues. In Europe, specialized toxicology wards were established in the late 1940s, with early examples in Copenhagen and Budapest. The Netherlands also initiated a poison information service. In the United States, the first poison information center was founded in Chicago in 1953. By 1957, there were 17 poison control centers across the U.S., modeled after the Chicago center. Initially, these centers primarily served physicians, providing information on product ingredients, toxicity, and treatment recommendations. Over time, they expanded their services to the general public. Most poison control centers were not physically integrated into treatment facilities but functioned as information hubs. In 1958, the American Association of Poison Control Centers (AAPCC) was established to foster collaboration among centers and standardize their operations. The AAPCC also launched poison prevention and education initiatives targeting both healthcare providers and the public. In 1968, the American Academy of Clinical Toxicologists (AACT) was formed by a group of physicians to advance the application of toxicology principles in patient care and to elevate national standards of care. The 1960s and 1970s saw a rapid increase in the number of poison centers, with 661 centers operating in the U.S. by 1978. By 2000, only 51 certified centers remained in the U.S. In Europe, the development of poison control systems followed a slightly different trajectory. Many European centers were centralized toxicology treatment facilities that also housed poison information services. For example, France established an inpatient unit for managing poisoned patients in the late 1950s. In England, the National Poison Information Service was created at Guy's Hospital under the leadership of Dr. Roy Goulding, while Dr. Henry Mathew founded a poison treatment center in Edinburgh. In 1964, the European Association for Poison Control Centers was established in Tours, France. Similarly, poison control centers were developed in Australasia during the 1960s. In the United States today, the AAPCC oversees a 24-hour national hotline staffed by pharmacists, physicians, nurses, and poison information specialists with specialized training in toxicology. The hotline also includes a TTY/TDD service for individuals with hearing impairments. Poison educators across the country provide community-based training and distribute educational materials to promote poison prevention. The national hotline number, 1-800-222-1222, connects callers to their nearest poison control center. Globally, most countries operate poison control centers with staffing and functions similar to those in the U.S. The World Health Organization maintains a comprehensive directory of poison control centers worldwide, which is accessible on its website. Local poison control centers in the U.S. include a wide range of facilities, such as the Alabama Poison Center, Arizona Poison and Drug Information Center, California Poison Control System, and many others. These centers are distributed across states and regions, ensuring widespread access to poison management resources. Additionally, specialized centers, such as the Animal Poison Control Center, cater to specific needs.
